title: The sakhis close
hookLine: the travels, the tests, the laughter and the lessons

lines: OIL GONE COOL. SOAPNUTS MADE SWEET.
A ROBBER SETS DOWN THE TREASURE.
cards: Boiling oil gone cool. A dead pipal tree turning green. Bitter soapnuts that tasted sweet.
A pot cooking on an eclipse day while the crowd shouted. A boy watching kindling catch. A robber setting down treasure because he'd tasted salt.

That's a lot of road for twenty-five days. This block opened the janamsakhis, the life-stories of Guru Nanak, and walked through them one sakhi at a time. Today we stop at the end of the road and look back.

teach.h: THE BOOKS, AND HOW TO READ THEM.
teach.b: Start with the books: the old Puratan telling, the Bala telling, Miharban's thoughtful one, the illustrated pages. We learned to read a sakhi not as a news report, but as truth in the shape of a story.
Then the people around Nanak: Mata Sulakhni, who kept the home going; Sri Chand, who chose a different path; parents in Talwandi asking him to stay.
Then the travels and the tests. Kauda and the oil. Mardana bewitched and sung free.
Bitter fruit made sweet. The yogis' seat. Cooking at the eclipse.
The learned man of Benares. Farid's verses kept at Pakpattan. The king of the island, waiting.
Then endings and beginnings: Mardana's last song and the rabab handed on, a boy by the fire who became Baba Buddha, two villages, settle here, scatter there, and Bhumia's three promises.

Last, how the sakhis live: differing in the details while the lesson stays, painted on walls, told aloud to children. Look across it all and a pattern shows. In these sakhis, the tests aren't won by force.
The oil cools, the robber keeps his word, the pandit listens to a song. And there's laughter in it: a Guru blessing the rude village to stay home.
Tomorrow the voices change. The Guru Granth Sahib holds the words of the Gurus and also of Bhagats, holy poets from different backgrounds. We met Kabir and Farid already.
Next, the Bhagats in their own voices.

how: Sikhs return to the sakhis of Guru Nanak's life in katha, at gurpurab celebrations and at home, and families have favorites they tell again.

games.q: a friend asks which sakhi from this block they should hear first. what do you do?
o: give them all of them at once.
tell them the one that tugs at you, and why.
tell them to read a history book instead.
games.why: today's carry: choose your favorite sakhi and tell someone why. a sakhi lives when someone tells it well.

practice: Let the sakhis pass by one at a time, like pictures on a wall: the oil, the soapnuts, Mardana's rabab, the boy and the kindling, the two villages, Bhumia and the salt.
Notice which one you keep coming back to, the one that tugs; that one is yours, and you can ask it what it knows that you need today. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath.
